edits.old: The assigned note connects the decision with sales-law modification rules. UCC § 2-209 removes the need for new consideration, but duress remains available through § 1-103(b), and Comment 2 to § 2-209 requires good faith. Thus, the consideration objection associated with Alaska Packers did not exhaust the analysis. The later Restatement §§ 175–176 framework maps coerced assent and absence of reasonable alternatives to § 175, and wrongful threatened breach to § 176(1)(d). Those are explanatory comparisons, not additional holdings in this appeal.
edits.new: The assigned note connects the decision with sales-law modification rules. UCC § 2-209 removes the need for new consideration, but duress remains available through § 1-103(b), and Comment 2 to § 2-209 requires good faith. Thus, the consideration objection associated with Alaska Packers did not exhaust the analysis. The later Restatement §§ 175–176 framework maps coerced assent and absence of reasonable alternatives to § 175, and a threatened breach that is itself a breach of the duty of good faith and fair dealing to § 176(1)(d). Those are explanatory comparisons, not additional holdings in this appeal.
edits.reason: Restatement § 176(1)(d) makes a threat improper only when the threat is a breach of the duty of good faith and fair dealing under a contract with the recipient; not every threatened breach qualifies.

edits.old: The later Restatement §§ 175–176 framework fits this case. Section 175 covers coerced "assent" (agreement forced by a threat) where there is no reasonable alternative, and § 176(1)(d) treats a wrongful threatened "breach" of contract as an improper threat.
edits.new: The later Restatement §§ 175–176 framework fits this case. Section 175 covers coerced "assent" (agreement forced by a threat) where there is no reasonable alternative, and § 176(1)(d) treats a threat as improper when the threat is itself a breach of the duty of "good faith and fair dealing" under the contract, as a threat to withhold owed deliveries to extract new terms may be.
edits.reason: Restatement § 176(1)(d) makes a threat improper only when the threat is a breach of the duty of good faith and fair dealing under a contract with the recipient; not every threatened breach qualifies.

edits.old: Normally a pressured party must "disaffirm," or reject, the forced deal promptly. But the pressure continued while Austin still owed critical deliveries under the second "subcontract," so objecting three days after the last delivery was soon enough.
edits.new: Normally a pressured party must "disaffirm," or reject, the forced deal promptly. But the pressure continued while Austin still owed critical deliveries under the second "subcontract," so demanding repayment three days after the last delivery was soon enough.
edits.reason: Loral protested in writing when it gave in (July 22); what it delayed was its demand for a refund.

edits.old: A pressured party may undo a contract if it agreed only because the other side made a wrongful threat that left it no real free choice.
edits.new: A pressured party may undo a contract if the other side's wrongful threat forced it to agree by leaving it no real free choice.
edits.reason: The court's test is that the party 'was forced to agree to it by means of a wrongful threat precluding the exercise of his free will'; it does not require that the threat be the only reason (Restatement § 175 comment c: substantially contributes).

edits.old: A contract modification is voidable for economic duress when a party threatens to withhold goods owed under a contract, and the threatened party cannot obtain them from another source in time and an ordinary action for breach would be inadequate.
edits.new: A contract modification is voidable for economic duress when a wrongful threat precluding free will, such as withholding owed goods unless a further demand is met, forces agreement, the threatened party cannot obtain the goods elsewhere in time, and an ordinary action for breach would be inadequate.
edits.reason: Austin's test requires that the party was forced to agree by a wrongful threat precluding the exercise of free will, the threat being to withhold goods unless the other party agrees to a further demand; the rule line dropped the inducement and the link between threat and demand.
edits.reviewDepth: Relevant assigned casebook, supplement, selections and slide passages checked by two workers and the lead; not a full-opinion or subsequent-treatment certification.

edits.old: Later Restatement § 89 can support some modifications without new consideration, but replacement difficulty alone does not establish unforeseen circumstances supporting a fair adjustment, and § 89(c) does not automatically protect every performance of an existing duty. New York General Obligations Law § 5-1103 can remove consideration objections to qualifying signed modifications without supplying authority or eliminating duress. Uniform Commercial Code § 2-209 applies to goods modifications; a crew’s services contract is not a goods sale merely because its employer sells salmon.
edits.new: Later Restatement § 89 can support some modifications without new consideration, but replacement difficulty alone does not establish circumstances not anticipated by the parties that would make an adjustment fair and equitable, and § 89(c) does not automatically protect every performance of an existing duty. New York General Obligations Law § 5-1103 can remove consideration objections to qualifying signed modifications without supplying authority or eliminating duress. Uniform Commercial Code § 2-209 applies to goods modifications; a crew’s services contract is not a goods sale merely because its employer sells salmon.
edits.reason: Restatement § 89(a) asks whether the modification is 'fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated by the parties when the contract was made'; comment b counts an event foreseen as a remote possibility if the contract did not adequately cover it, so 'events nobody expected' changes the test.
edits.reviewDepth: Relevant assigned casebook, supplement, selections and slide passages checked by two workers and the lead; not a full-opinion or subsequent-treatment certification.

edits.old: Restatement § 89, a later rule, can make some contract "modifications" (changes) binding without new consideration if fair and caused by "unforeseen circumstances," events nobody expected. Difficulty finding replacement workers alone does not qualify, and § 89(c) does not automatically protect every "performance" of a duty already owed.
edits.new: Restatement § 89, a later rule, can make a "modification" (change) of a contract not yet fully performed binding without new consideration if it is "fair and equitable" in view of circumstances the parties did not anticipate when they contracted. An event foreseen only as a remote possibility can count if the contract did not adequately cover it. Difficulty finding replacement workers alone does not qualify, and § 89(c) does not automatically protect every "performance" of a duty already owed.
edits.reason: Restatement § 89(a) asks whether the modification is 'fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated by the parties when the contract was made'; comment b counts an event foreseen as a remote possibility if the contract did not adequately cover it, so 'events nobody expected' changes the test.

edits.old: New York General Obligations Law § 5-1103 can remove "consideration" objections (that nothing new was exchanged) to qualifying signed, written "modifications" of a contract. But it does not give someone authority he lacked, and it does not cure duress, meaning improper pressure.
edits.new: New York General Obligations Law § 5-1103 can remove "consideration" objections (that nothing new was exchanged) to a written "modification" of a contract signed by the party against whom it is to be enforced, or by that party's agent. But it does not give someone authority he lacked, and it does not cure duress, meaning improper pressure.
edits.reason: N.Y. Gen. Oblig. Law § 5-1103 protects only a writing signed by the party against whom the change is to be enforced, or by that party's agent.

edits.old: A services modification may encounter the pre-existing-duty rule. Model UCC § 2-209 removes consideration as a requirement for a goods modification, while good faith still matters. New York’s signed-writing statute and the Restatement’s fair-modification approach offer distinct routes. None makes coercion irrelevant.
edits.new: A services modification may encounter the pre-existing-duty rule. Model UCC § 2-209 removes consideration as a requirement for a goods modification, but the modification must meet the Code’s test of good faith. New York’s statute for a writing signed by the party against whom the change is enforced and the Restatement’s fair-modification approach offer distinct routes. None makes coercion irrelevant.
edits.reason: UCC § 2-209 comment 2 makes good faith a requirement ('must meet the test of good faith'), and § 5-1103 requires the signature of the party to be charged.

edits.old: The casebook compares Schwartzreich, where parties tore signatures from the old salary agreement and signed a replacement. Watkins did not require that ceremony. Later Restatement § 89 comment b criticized simultaneous rescission as a fiction and instead tested a modification’s fairness and justification directly. Its first illustration uses the cellar, unexpected rock, and nine-times rate to reach a binding modification when reasonable. That later route was not the rule Allen applied and does not erase his conclusion that mutual mistake failed. An event can leave the initial obligation intact yet support a consensual adjustment.
edits.new: The casebook compares Schwartzreich, where parties tore signatures from the old salary agreement and signed a replacement. Watkins did not require that ceremony. Later Restatement § 89 comment b rejected simultaneous rescission as a fiction and instead asked directly whether a modification is fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated when the contract was made. Its first illustration uses the cellar, unexpected rock, and nine-times rate to reach a binding modification when reasonable. That later route was not the rule Allen applied and does not erase his conclusion that mutual mistake failed. An event can leave the initial obligation intact yet support a consensual adjustment.
edits.reason: Restatement § 89 comment b says 'That theory is rejected here'; the § 89(a) test is fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated.

edits.old: In Austin a gear supplier withheld indispensable supply while Loral could not timely replace it and faced Navy obligations. Test market alternatives, timing, inducement and whether apparent acquiescence continued under the pressure.
edits.new: In Austin a gear supplier withheld indispensable supply while Loral could not timely replace it and faced Navy obligations. Test market alternatives, whether an ordinary action for breach would be adequate, timing, inducement and whether apparent acquiescence continued under the pressure.
edits.reason: Austin requires, besides the wrongful threat and no other timely source, that 'the ordinary remedy of an action for breach of contract would not be adequate.'

edits.old: The coerced party may avoid the modification and seek appropriate recovery. Continued performance or a delay in protesting can be consistent with ongoing pressure, as in Austin.
edits.new: The coerced party may avoid the modification and seek appropriate recovery. The coerced party must disaffirm promptly once the pressure ends. In Austin, Loral protested in writing when it gave in and could wait to demand a refund until three days after the last delivery, because further stoppages remained possible until then.
edits.reason: Loral did not delay its protest (letter of July 22); the court required one who would recover money paid under duress to 'act promptly' and excused only the wait for the refund demand while further compulsion was possible.
edits.reviewDepth: Relevant assigned casebook, supplement, selections and slide passages checked by two workers and the lead; not a full-opinion or subsequent-treatment certification.

edits.reason: Restatement § 89(c) and comment d enforce a modification, otherwise not binding, to the extent justice requires because of reliance.

edits.old: Slide 5 quotes Restatement § 73: performing a legal duty owed to the promisor that is neither doubtful nor in honest dispute is not consideration. Mutual promises to rescind are supported by consideration, so the rule does not stop parties from rescinding and replacing a contract, and a modification supported by even minimal consideration is enforceable.
edits.new: Slide 5 quotes Restatement § 73: performing a legal duty owed to the promisor that is neither doubtful nor in honest dispute is not consideration. Mutual promises to rescind are supported by consideration, so the rule does not stop parties from rescinding and replacing a contract, and a modification supported by even minimal consideration is enforceable under the pre-existing duty rule.
edits.reason: Slide 5 reads 'will be enforceable under the pre-existing duty rule'; without the qualifier the note says minimal consideration makes any modification enforceable, which duress (Austin) and UCC § 2-209 comment 2 contradict.

edits.old: Separately, Illinois "promissory-fraud" doctrine (fraud based on a broken promise about the future) required a "fraudulent scheme", a larger plan to cheat. Proof of more than the allegedly false promise itself was needed, and Speakers showed none.
edits.new: Separately, Illinois "promissory-fraud" doctrine (fraud based on a promise the promisor did not intend to keep when making it) required a "fraudulent scheme", a larger plan to cheat. Proof of more than the allegedly false promise itself was needed, and Speakers showed none.
edits.reason: Promissory fraud is a promise the promisor did not intend to perform when making it; a promise that is merely not performed is a simple breach (C&M 519). The scheme must be 'evidenced by more than the allegedly fraudulent promise itself' (C&M 523).
edits.reviewDepth: Relevant assigned casebook, supplement, selections and slide passages checked by two workers and the lead; not a full-opinion or subsequent-treatment certification.

edits.old: Aspirational sales talk is puffery, not fraud, and Illinois promissory fraud needs a scheme to defraud beyond one broken promise.

edits.reason: Promissory fraud is a promise the promisor did not intend to perform when making it; a promise that is merely not performed is a simple breach (C&M 519). The scheme must be 'evidenced by more than the allegedly fraudulent promise itself' (C&M 523).

edits.old: The related sports-agency dispute in Speakers of Sport v. ProServ shows how context matters. That court "construed" (interpreted) a forecast of endorsement deals as aspirational sales talk, and separately applied Illinois's special requirement for fraud claims based on a fraudulent scheme.
edits.new: The related sports-agency dispute in Speakers of Sport v. ProServ shows how context matters. That court "construed" (interpreted) a forecast of endorsement deals as aspirational sales talk, and separately applied Illinois's requirement that a claim of promissory fraud (a promise made without intent to keep it) show a scheme to defraud beyond the promise itself.
edits.reason: The scheme requirement applies to a promise said to be fraudulent, not to fraud claims generally.
edits.reviewDepth: Relevant assigned casebook, supplement, selections and slide passages checked by two workers and the lead; not a full-opinion or subsequent-treatment certification.

edits.old: The Seventh Circuit read ProServ's pitch as aspirational "puffery", the kind of sales hype no one takes literally. ProServ was saying it would try to get endorsements and was optimistic about the result, not guaranteeing it.
edits.new: The Seventh Circuit read ProServ's pitch as aspirational "puffery": a sales pitch that a reasonable person in Rodriguez's position would understand as an expression of hope rather than an enforceable commitment. ProServ was saying it would try to get endorsements and was optimistic about the result, not guaranteeing it.
edits.reason: Posner rejected the 'cascade of extravagant adjectives' sense of puffing: the test is a pitch the speaker intends, and a reasonable person in the promisee's position would understand, to be aspirational rather than enforceable.
edits.reviewDepth: Relevant assigned casebook, supplement, selections and slide passages checked by two workers and the lead; not a full-opinion or subsequent-treatment certification.

edits.old: Telling an athlete you will get him millions in endorsements is sales talk, not a promise, when third parties decide whether to sign him. Competing for a client who can leave at any time is allowed unless you use fraud or other unlawful means.
edits.new: Telling an athlete you will get him millions in endorsements was sales talk: a reasonable athlete would hear hope that the agent would try, not a guarantee, though a party can bind itself to a result others control. Competing for a client who can leave at any time is allowed unless you use fraud or other unlawful means.
edits.reason: The court said a party can make a binding promise of something it does not control (a warranty); the outcome turned on what the statement reasonably conveyed, with third-party control one reason for that reading.

edits.old: Under the Massachusetts rule applied in 1942, merely staying silent about termites did not support this tort claim. There had to be a misleading statement, concealment, or duty to disclose. Other jurisdictions and later statutes may require disclosure. This decision is not a universal current rule allowing sellers to hide home defects.
edits.new: Under the Massachusetts rule applied in 1942, merely staying silent about termites did not support this tort claim. There had to be a misleading statement, active concealment that prevented the buyer from learning the facts, or a duty to disclose. Other jurisdictions and later statutes may require disclosure. This decision is not a universal current rule allowing sellers to hide home defects.
edits.reason: Swinton pleaded concealment and lost: 'concealment in the simple sense of mere failure to reveal' is not enough; the court looked for conduct that prevented the buyer from acquiring information.

edits.reason: Swinton decided a demurrer to a Massachusetts tort declaration in 1942; it named half-truths, conduct preventing the buyer from acquiring information, a fiduciary relation or relation of confidence or dependence, and any peculiar duty to speak; the notes report courts and a statute requiring disclosure.

edits.old: Justice Cutter's opinion for the Supreme Judicial Court, Massachusetts's highest court, assumed that complete silence might have put the cases under Swinton. Swinton was a precedent holding that mere "nondisclosure" (failing to mention a fact) is not fraud.
edits.new: Justice Cutter's opinion for the Supreme Judicial Court, Massachusetts's highest court, assumed that complete silence might have put the cases under Swinton. Swinton was a precedent holding that a seller's bare "nondisclosure" (failing to mention a fact), in an arm's-length deal with no fiduciary relationship or other special duty to speak, did not support the buyer's tort claim.
edits.reason: Swinton reserved fiduciary relations, relations of confidence or dependence and any peculiar duty to speak; 'nondisclosure is not fraud' states the rule without them.

edits.old: "Superior knowledge" by the speaker, the listener's trust, unequal ability to judge the subject, and "devices" (tricks) making an opinion misleading could support "relief." That was so even when the statements were framed as opinions.

edits.old: Apply waiver, prevention and disproportionate forfeiture where supported. Also ask whether there was an independent promise to produce the event, whose breach may support damages.
edits.new: Apply waiver and prevention where supported. edits.reason: § 229 lets a court excuse a condition to avoid disproportionate forfeiture 'unless its occurrence was a material part of the agreed exchange'; without that limit K-27 excused Kingston's security condition and gave Nelson's builder the full price (C&M 824, 830).

edits.old: Under § 89 a modification of a contract not fully performed on either side binds if fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated when the contract was made, to the extent a statute provides (UCC § 2-209 and N.Y. edits.new: Under § 89 a modification of a contract not fully performed on either side binds if fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated when the contract was made, to the extent a statute provides (UCC § 2-209 and N.Y. Gen. Oblig. L. § 5-1103 remove the consideration requirement), or to the extent justice requires because of a material change of position in reliance. Legal qualification: UCC § 2-209(1) removes the consideration requirement only for modifications of contracts within Article 2 (goods), and the modification must still meet the Code's test of good faith (comment 2); N.Y. Gen. Oblig. L. § 5-1103 applies only to a modification in writing signed by the party against whom it is enforced or by that party's agent. Modifications may also be enforced as waivers, but only until retracted unless relied on.

edits.old: Duress requires an improper threat, which once meant unlawful confinement or bodily harm and now extends to property and economic harm, including breach of contract and a threat to breach the duty of good faith; the absence of a reasonable alternative; and unfair terms, which matter less if the threat is improper enough. A threat to breach “without legitimate commercial reason” can be a breach of the duty of good faith (UCC § 2-209, comment 2).
edits.new: Duress requires an improper threat, which once meant unlawful confinement or bodily harm and now extends to property and economic harm, including breach of contract and a threat to breach the duty of good faith; the absence of a reasonable alternative; and unfair terms, which matter less if the threat is improper enough. Legal qualification: Restatement § 175(1) does not list unfair terms as an element; they are required only for threats that are improper under § 176(2), while a threat listed in § 176(1), such as a threat to breach the duty of good faith and fair dealing, is improper whatever the terms. A threat to breach “without legitimate commercial reason” can be a breach of the duty of good faith (UCC § 2-209, comment 2).

edits.old: Slide 8's table maps Restatement and UCC § 2-202 terms. A partially integrated (“final”) writing discharges prior inconsistent agreements (§§ 213(1), 215) but can be supplemented by consistent additional terms (§ 216(1)). A completely integrated (“final, complete and exclusive”) writing also discharges prior consistent agreements within its scope (§ 213(2)) and cannot be supplemented by consistent additional terms within its scope; under UCC § 2-202(a), course of performance, course of dealing and usage of trade may still explain or supplement it. A merger clause is relevant to the extent of integration but not dispositive, and parol evidence can still challenge the validity of a completely integrated agreement.
edits.new: Slide 8's table maps Restatement and UCC § 2-202 terms. A partially integrated (“final”) writing discharges prior inconsistent agreements (§§ 213(1), 215) but can be supplemented by consistent additional terms (§ 216(1)). A completely integrated (“final, complete and exclusive”) writing also discharges prior consistent agreements within its scope (§ 213(2)) and cannot be supplemented by consistent additional terms within its scope; under UCC § 2-202(a), course of performance, course of dealing and usage of trade may still explain or supplement it. A merger clause is relevant to the extent of integration but not dispositive, and parol evidence can still challenge the validity of a completely integrated agreement. Legal qualification: courts are split on merger clauses. Some treat the clause as conclusive proof that the writing is completely integrated, while others treat it as strong but rebuttable evidence (C&M 542).
edits.reason: Slide 9 states the 'not dispositive' position; C&M 542 reports a split, with Howard v. Perry and Phelps-Dickson treating the clause as conclusive (OP-CT-13 challenge item 25(a)).

edits.old: First establish the right. Then identify a contractual reservation and the governing effect of assent, material reliance, or suit before the attempted change.

Unless a term of the promise forbids it, the parties may discharge or modify the duty by later agreement (§ 311(2)); that power ends if, before notice of the change, the beneficiary materially changed position in justifiable reliance, sued, or assented at the promisor's or promisee's request (§ 311(3)).

The node listed any assent and spoke of a 'reservation', the First Restatement rule (C&M 1195).

Chicago Flame Hardening, C&M 1195). A creditor beneficiary keeps any claim against the promisee on the original debt, because delegating payment did not discharge it (§ 318(3)).

edits.old: In Lawrence, paying the creditor would satisfy the promisee’s debt. In Seaver, the husband’s promised provision by will was directed to the niece. Look for objective intent to confer enforceable benefit under the local rule.

Under Restatement § 302, the claimant is intended only if a right is appropriate to effectuate the parties' intention and either (a) performance will satisfy the promisee's duty to pay the claimant money, even a time-barred duty, or (b) the promisee intends to give the claimant the benefit; otherwise the claimant is incidental. Apply any different local rule.

edits.old: The assignor held the right, the assignee seeks it, and the obligor owes performance. Check transfer language, contractual restrictions, notice and defenses. Hamer’s claimant held an assigned right. Masterson concerned an alleged restriction on an option’s assignability.
edits.new: The assignor held the right, the assignee seeks it, and the obligor owes performance. Check transfer language, notice and defenses. A right cannot be assigned if substituting the assignee would materially change the obligor's duty or materially increase its burden or risk, if a statute or public policy forbids it, or if the contract validly precludes it (§ 317(2); UCC § 2-210(2)). Unless it shows a different intention, a term barring assignment of rights gives the obligor damages but does not make the assignment ineffective (§ 322(2)(b)); a ban on assigning 'the contract' bars only delegation (§ 322(1)). Hamer’s claimant held an assigned right. Masterson concerned an alleged restriction on an option’s assignability.
edits.reason: § 322(2)(b): a term barring assignment of rights 'does not render the assignment ineffective'; § 317(2)(a) and the oil example at C&M 1226–1227 bar a materially burdensome assignment. The node sent any contractual restriction to 'Transfer ineffective'.

edits.old:
Section 9 is one sentence. It works by denying the standard term the status the parol-evidence rule depends on: the term is not treated as a final expression on that subject, so there is no integration to discharge the business's prior affirmation or promise.

Comment 1 states the reason. Standard terms are not a jointly drafted memorial of a negotiated agreement, so there is less reason to let them override what the consumer was told. It describes § 9 as a corollary of § 7 (deception) and § 8 (affirmations and promises are part of the contract and cannot be negated by standard terms).

Read with Restatement (Second) §§ 209–216 and UCC § 2-202 from the same assignment: those ask whether a writing is integrated; § 9 answers that question against the business for a standard term that conflicts with its own earlier statement.

edits.old:
(a) The business's own affirmation or promise becomes part of the contract when it creates a reasonable expectation, in a consumer who is the intended audience, that the subject matter will have a particular attribute.

(b) A third party's affirmation or promise of that kind (1) becomes part of the contract between the business and the consumer if the business knew or reasonably should have known of it and the consumer could reasonably have believed the business intended to stand behind it; and (2) binds the third party itself to the consumer, even without a direct transaction, if the third party has an appreciable financial interest in the contract.

(c) Standard contract terms that purport to negate or unreasonably limit obligations arising under (a) and (b) are not enforceable.

The syllabus lists § 8 twice: with the parol-evidence rule (Assignment 13, alongside § 9) and with standard forms and adhesion (Assignment 17).

Each section opens at its own page from the source buttons. Sections 4, 6, 8 and 9 also have their own entries on the Contracts map, in the subtopic of the assignment that lists them.

§ 2. Adoption of standard terms (Assignments 6, 9). (a) A standard term is adopted if the business shows the consumer manifested assent to the transaction after reasonable notice of the term and of the intent to include it, and a reasonable opportunity to review it. (b) For terms available only after assent: reasonable advance notice that terms will follow, of the opportunity to review and terminate, and that not terminating adopts them; a reasonable opportunity to review afterwards; and a reasonable opportunity to terminate without unreasonable cost, loss of value or personal burden, not exercised. (c) A contract is not unenforceable because some standard terms were not adopted; its terms are those adopted, any unadopted standard terms the consumer elects, terms both parties agreed to, and terms supplied by law.

§ 3. Modification of standard terms (Assignment 11). (a) In an ongoing relationship a proposed modification is adopted only if the business shows reasonable notice of the modified term and opportunity to review it; a reasonable, noticed opportunity to reject it and continue under the existing term; reasonable notice that continuing without rejecting adopts it; and either assent or continued use after the rejection period. (b) The contract may set a reasonable modification procedure, which may substitute a reasonable opportunity to terminate for the opportunity to reject, but may not otherwise exclude (a) to the consumer's detriment. (c) The modification must be proposed in good faith, be fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated at contracting, and not undermine an affirmation or promise that was part of the basis of the original bargain. (d) Standard terms may not be modified once the contract has been substantially performed by at least one party.

§ 4, § 6, § 8, § 9: see their own entries.

Not assigned: § 1 (definitions and scope), § 5 (discretionary obligations), § 7 (deception), § 10 (derogation from mandatory provisions).

§ 2. Adoption of standard terms (Assignments 6, 9). (a) A standard term is adopted if the business shows the consumer manifested assent to the transaction after reasonable notice of the term and of the intent to include it, and a reasonable opportunity to review it. (b) For terms available only after assent: reasonable advance notice that terms will follow, of the opportunity to review and terminate, and that not terminating adopts them; a reasonable opportunity to review afterwards; and a reasonable opportunity to terminate without unreasonable cost, loss of value or personal burden, not exercised. (c) A contract is not unenforceable because some standard terms were not adopted; its terms are those adopted, any unadopted standard terms the consumer elects, terms both parties agreed to, and terms supplied by law.

§ 3. Modification of standard terms (Assignment 11). (a) In an ongoing relationship a proposed modification is adopted only if the business shows reasonable notice of the modified term and opportunity to review it; a reasonable, noticed opportunity to reject it and continue under the existing term; reasonable notice that continuing without rejecting adopts it; and either assent or continued use after the rejection period. (b) The contract may set a reasonable modification procedure, which may substitute a reasonable opportunity to terminate for the opportunity to reject, but may not otherwise exclude (a) to the consumer's detriment. (c) The modification must be proposed in good faith, be fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated at contracting, and not undermine an affirmation or promise that was part of the basis of the original bargain. (d) Standard terms may not be modified once the contract has been substantially performed by at least one party.

edits.new: Renner concerned water already unavailable in the necessary quantity for jojoba cultivation. Test basic assumption, material effect and whether the party seeking relief bears the risk (§ 154). Material effect means an imbalance so severe that the party cannot fairly be required to perform, ordinarily because the exchange is both less desirable to him and more advantageous to the other party (§ 152 cmt. c). If only one party was mistaken, that party may avoid only if those requirements are met and, in addition, enforcement would be unconscionable or the other party had reason to know of the mistake or his fault caused it (§ 153); erroneous construction bids are the usual case (Elsinore, C&M 1081). A fact existing at formation that made performance impracticable, or substantially frustrated the principal purpose, may instead excuse under § 266.

edits.old: Read actual assumption of risk, contractual clauses, and the allocation implied by the deal and law. Stees construed the building promise strictly despite quicksand. For force majeure, apply trigger, causation, notice, mitigation and relief specified by the language.
edits.new: Read actual assumption of risk, contractual clauses, and the allocation implied by the deal and law. For mistake, a party bears the risk when the agreement allocates it, when he knew at formation that his knowledge was limited and treated it as sufficient (conscious ignorance), or when the court allocates it as reasonable (§ 154); courts generally allocate to a seller of farm land the risk that it holds valuable minerals (C&M 1081 Note 2) and to a builder the cost of draining subsoil (§ 154 illus. 5). Stees construed the building promise strictly despite quicksand; where the owner supplied a design specification prescribing design, materials and methods, courts treat it as impliedly warranting their adequacy (Spearin, C&M 1077 Note 2). For force majeure, apply trigger, causation, notice, mitigation and relief specified by the language: general words after a list may be confined to similar events (ejusdem generis), a clause covering an event may not cover its economic aftermath, and an express exclusion such as a duty to pay rent regardless controls (C&M 1117–1119).
edits.reason: § 154 allocates the risk by agreement, by conscious ignorance ('aware ... that he has only limited knowledge ... but treats his limited knowledge as sufficient'), or by the court; Stees Note 2 says a design specification 'impliedly warrants their adequacy' (C&M 1077); the force-majeure notes turn on ejusdem generis, economic aftermath and a rent proviso (C&M 1117–1119). Node d named none of these.

edits.new: Taylor’s particular music hall burned without fault. That excuse applies when a specific existing thing that performance requires is destroyed: a contractor repairing an existing building that burns is discharged (§ 261 illus. 6; § 263), but a builder whose own unfinished building is destroyed without his fault must ordinarily rebuild (Stees Note 3, C&M 1077–1078). Transatlantic’s Cape route still allowed performance at greater cost. Check fault, available alternatives, foreseeability as evidence of allocation, basic assumption and contractual risk. Under § 261 the event must occur without the party's fault, which includes negligence and breach; market shifts and a party's financial inability are ordinarily not events whose non-occurrence was a basic assumption; and impracticability means extreme and unreasonable difficulty, expense, injury or loss despite reasonable efforts, more than 'impracticality' (cmts. b, d).

edits.old: The canceled coronation procession was the shared foundation for the particular rooms in Krell. Check severity, shared understanding, fault and who bore the risk. Ordinary disappointment or reduced profits will seldom suffice.
edits.new: In Krell the processions' taking place on the proclaimed days, along the proclaimed route past the rooms, was the foundation of the license to use them, as both parties regarded it (C&M 1134). Check severity, shared understanding, fault and who bore the risk. Knowing the other party's purpose is not enough: the object must be so completely the basis of the contract that, as both understand, without it the transaction would make little sense, and a less profitable transaction or even a loss does not suffice (§ 265 cmt. a). In Krell's Derby Day dictum, a cab hired at an enhanced price to go to the race is not discharged when the race is cancelled, because the cab 'had no special qualification for this particular occasion' (C&M 1134).
edits.reason: Vaughan Williams L.J.: 'the taking place of those processions on the days proclaimed along the proclaimed route, which passed 56A, Pall Mall' was the foundation, while the Derby Day cab 'had no special qualification for this particular occasion' (C&M 1134); § 265 cmt. a: a loss 'is not enough'. Node f let a known purpose reach discharge, so the cab hirer was discharged, and said reduced profit will 'seldom' suffice.

edits.old: Mistake can justify avoidance and restoration. A later event may discharge or suspend remaining duties, depending on doctrine or clause. Renner restored payment and net value conferred, rather than every development expense.
edits.new: Mistake can justify avoidance and restoration (§§ 158, 376). A later event may discharge or suspend remaining duties, depending on doctrine or clause; a temporary impediment suspends the duty and discharges it only if later performance would be materially more burdensome (§ 269). After discharge, either party may claim restitution for benefits conferred by part performance or reliance (§§ 272(1), 377), and a court may protect reliance where those rules will not avoid injustice (§§ 158(2), 272(2)). Renner, applying Arizona law, restored payment and net value conferred, rather than every development expense. Taylor's promoters could not recover preparation expenses as damages for breach (C&M 1105), and Transatlantic said that a carrier whose contract was a nullity would claim quantum meruit for the entire voyage, not only the extra cost on top of the collected price (C&M 1112).
edits.reason: § 272(1) and § 377 give restitution for benefits conferred by part performance or reliance after discharge, and §§ 158(2), 272(2) let a court protect reliance only where those rules 'will not avoid injustice'; Transatlantic: the claim 'should have been quantum meruit for the entire trip, rather than only for the extra expense' (C&M 1112). Node g gave no rule for relief after discharge.

edits.old: A party who makes a positive, express promise must perform it despite unforeseen hindrance or hardship unless performance is prevented by an act of God, the law or the other party; difficulty short of absolute impossibility is no excuse.
edits.new: Minnesota's 1874 rule: one who expressly promises a possible act must perform despite hardship or unforeseen hindrance unless prevented by an act of God, the law or the other party, and difficulty short of absolute impossibility is no excuse. Restatement § 261 later recognized discharge for impracticability.
edits.reason: Young, J.'s 1874 formulation ('No hardship, no unforeseen hindrance, no difficulty short of absolute impossibility, will excuse him', C&M 1075) was stated as present law; Transatlantic says the doctrine 'has gradually been freed from the earlier ... strictures' and § 261 cmt. d discharges 'even though the event has not made performance absolutely impossible' (C&M 1108–1109).

edits.reason: Renner awarded the down payment plus enhancement of the land's value, less fair rental value (C&M 1080–1081); development spending counted to the extent it enhanced the land.

edits.old: Its second footnote stressed that the buyers' failure to investigate thoroughly did not by itself defeat "rescission." The contract had not put that risk on them, and the shared "mistake" concerned a material "basic assumption."
edits.new: Its second footnote stressed that the parties' failure to investigate the water supply thoroughly before signing did not by itself defeat "rescission" when the risk of the mistake had not been allocated among them and the shared "mistake" concerned a material "basic assumption." A party bears that risk if the agreement assigns it, if he knowingly treats limited knowledge as sufficient, or if a court reasonably assigns it to him (§ 154).
edits.reason: Footnote 2: failure to investigate 'prior to signing the contract does not preclude rescission where the risk of mistake was not allocated among the parties' (C&M 1079). The plain sentence turned that condition into a finding that 'the contract' had not put the risk on the buyers, omitting conscious ignorance and court allocation (§ 154(b)–(c)).

edits.old: The parties’ bargain depended on this music hall’s continued existence, which the owners had not guaranteed. Its faultless destruction excused the promised concert performance, and the promoters could not recover their preparation losses. edits.reason: Blackburn J.: 'both parties are excused, the plaintiffs from taking the gardens and paying the money, the defendants from performing their promise to give the use of the Hall' (C&M 1105); no one promised a 'concert performance'.

edits.old: A contract excuse: an unexpected event destroys the deal's main purpose, known to both sides, so duties end though performance remains possible. In English law, frustration also covers impossibility.
edits.new: A contract excuse: after formation, an unexpected event without the party's fault substantially frustrates a principal purpose that both sides understood as the basis of the deal, so remaining duties end though performance remains possible (Restatement § 265). Knowledge of the purpose alone is not enough. In English law, frustration also covers impossibility.
edits.reason: 'Known to both sides' is not enough: the Derby Day cab hirer's purpose is known yet he is not discharged (C&M 1134), and § 265 cmt. a requires that 'as both parties understand, without it the transaction would make little sense'.

edits.old: A defense excusing contract performance when an unexpected event, not the party's fault, makes performing far more difficult or costly than anyone assumed.

edits.reason: 'Far more difficult or costly than anyone assumed' omits the basic-assumption element and suggests cost alone suffices; § 261 cmt. d: 'impracticability' means more than 'impracticality', and UCC § 2-615 cmt. 4: 'Increased cost alone does not excuse performance'.

edits.old: Use reasonable correction cost where supported. Weigh waste, proportionality and whether the breached undertaking was central. Groves favored restoration cost. Peevyhouse used $300 diminution for restoration it treated as incidental. Plante selected repair costs by defect.
edits.new: Start from the loss in value to this owner (§ 347(a)). If that loss is not proved with sufficient certainty, § 348(2) allows damages based on the drop in market price or on the reasonable cost to complete or repair, but cost only if it is not clearly disproportionate to the probable loss in value to the owner. Plante (Wisconsin) allowed repair cost for small defects fixable without unreasonable economic waste, but valued the misplaced wall by diminution, which was zero: moving it ($4,000) would destroy finished work, and it did not affect market price. Groves (Minnesota) gave the reasonable cost of grading wilfully left undone, even above the graded land’s value, treating economic waste as only the wrecking of a completed structure and citing precedent that applies repair cost to remediable defects even after good-faith substantial performance. Peevyhouse (Oklahoma) held that reasonable cost of performance ordinarily governs, but limited the owners to the $300 diminution because both conditions held: the restoration term was merely incidental to the lease’s main purpose, and its economic benefit was grossly disproportionate to its cost.
edits.reason: For Plante's wall the $4,000 relocation cost was proved, yet the court allowed nothing: the wall fell 'clearly under the diminished-value rule' and did not affect market price (C&M 970–971). The node also omitted § 348(2)(b)'s 'not clearly disproportionate' limit, Peevyhouse's two conjunctive conditions (C&M 980–981) and Groves's wilfulness and Snider grounds (C&M 975, 977).
edits.reviewDepth: Relevant assigned casebook, supplement, selections and slide passages checked by two workers and the lead; not a full-opinion or subsequent-treatment certification.

edits.old: Under Algernon Blair’s rule a nonbreaching contractor may recover reasonable value despite a losing deal. If the work in the illustration was worth $55 to supply at reasonable rates, that measure may be $55, with no duplicate recovery and subject to proof.
edits.new: Under Algernon Blair’s rule a nonbreaching contractor that justifiably stopped after part performance may recover reasonable value despite a losing deal. If the work in the illustration was worth $55 to supply at reasonable rates, that measure may be $55, with no duplicate recovery and subject to proof. Restitution is not available to a contractor that has performed all its duties when only a definite sum of money remains due; it recovers the unpaid price, and a full performer cannot recover more than the price (§ 373(2); C&M 992).
edits.reason: § 373(2): 'The injured party has no right to restitution if he has performed all of his duties under the contract and no performance by the other party remains due other than payment of a definite sum of money'; Note 2: a full performer 'cannot recover more than the contract price', and courts divide on a ceiling after part performance (C&M 992).

edits.old: Restitution is a broad term for recovery based on unjust enrichment. It is commonly awarded for mistaken payments, implied contracts, contracts avoided for misrepresentation, and contracts whose performance is excused by breach, impossibility or non-occurrence of a condition. Recovery may be measured by the cost of the goods or services or by how far they increased the value of the defendant's property or advanced the defendant's interests.
edits.new: Restitution is a broad term for recovery based on unjust enrichment. It is commonly awarded for mistaken payments, implied contracts, contracts avoided for misrepresentation, and contracts whose performance is excused by breach, impossibility or non-occurrence of a condition. Recovery may be measured by the cost of the goods or services or by how far they increased the value of the defendant's property or advanced the defendant's interests. Legal qualification: restitution measures the benefit the defendant received, not the claimant's loss (C&M 145); under Restatement (Second) § 371(a) the cost is what it would have cost the defendant to obtain the benefit from someone in the claimant's position, and “implied contracts” in this list is best read as contracts implied in law (quasi-contract), a claim for unjust enrichment rather than on a true contract (C&M 146).
edits.reason: Slide 3's 'cost of the goods or services' can read as the claimant's outlay; § 371(a) measures 'the reasonable value to the other party of what he received in terms of what it would have cost him to obtain it from a person in the claimant's position', and restitution 'derives from the receipt of a benefit' (C&M 145).
edits.reviewDepth: Relevant assigned casebook, supplement, selections and slide passages checked by two workers and the lead; not a full-opinion or subsequent-treatment certification.

edits.old: The Chicago officer’s O.K. was the prescribed act in International Filter. Carlill invited completed performance without advance notice. Where the offeror may not promptly learn of performance, test whether reasonable notice is required.
edits.new: An acceptance by promise must be communicated unless the offer manifests a contrary intention (§ 56). International Filter's order said it 'becomes a contract when' approved by an executive officer at the Chicago office, so the officer's O.K. accepted without separate notice (C&M 219–220); the casebook asks how that result fits the notice rule (C&M 221, 227), and the court found the answer in the offer's own terms. For an offer inviting performance, the performance is the acceptance and needs no notification unless the offer requests it (§ 54(1)); in Carlill, performing the condition was a sufficient acceptance without notification (C&M 228). If the offeree has reason to know the offeror cannot learn of the performance promptly and with certainty, the offeror's duty is discharged unless the offeree uses reasonable diligence to notify, the offeror learns of it within a reasonable time, or the offer says notice is not required (§ 54(2); Bishop v. Eaton, C&M 229).

edits.old: Eel-skin shipments repeatedly accepted in Hobbs and the settled order-and-production practice in American Bronze made conduct and silence probative. Unsolicited goods ordinarily do not impose acceptance by inaction.
edits.new: Eel-skin shipments repeatedly accepted in Hobbs and the settled order-and-production practice in American Bronze made conduct and silence probative. Unsolicited goods ordinarily do not impose acceptance by inaction. Silence accepts only in the cases § 69(1) lists: the offeree takes offered services with a reasonable chance to reject them and reason to know they were offered for pay; the offeror has said silence may signify assent and the offeree, staying silent, intends to accept; or previous dealings make it reasonable for the offeree to give notice of non-acceptance. An offeror cannot use such a statement to hold an offeree who merely fails to reject (C&M 235). An offeree who acts inconsistently with the offeror's ownership of offered property is bound on the offered terms unless they are manifestly unreasonable (§ 69(2)), though statutes can make unsolicited goods a gift (C&M 236).
edits.reason: § 69(1) lists the cases in which silence accepts ('in the following cases only'), including (b) an offeror's statement that silence may signify assent where the offeree, silent, intends to accept; § 69(2) binds an offeree who uses offered property. The casebook rule that an offeror who appends 'Unless I hear from you' cannot hold an offeree who fails to reject protects the offeree (C&M 235); a recipient who shelves unsolicited goods incurs no liability, and N.Y. Gen. Bus. L. § 396 makes them a gift (C&M 236).

edits.old: An offeror may dispense with notice of acceptance by authorizing a particular act as sufficient acceptance; the offeree then completes the contract by performing that specified act, without separately communicating it.
edits.new: An offeror may dispense with notice of acceptance, and does so when the offer's terms show notice is unnecessary (compare § 56); an order stating that it 'becomes a contract when' approved by the seller's executive officer at Chicago is accepted by that approval without separate notice.
edits.reason: The court held the offeror may dispense with notification and 'does dispense with it "if the form of th[e offer] ... shows that this was not to be required"'; it found that showing in the order's terms that it 'becomes a contract when' approved by an executive officer at Chicago (C&M 219–220). The editors treat the result as needing reconciliation with § 56's notice rule for acceptance by promise (C&M 221 Note 4, 227). Stated as 'authorizing a particular act', the rule let an approval clause with no dispensing terms bind the buyer without notice.

edits.old: An acceptance is a manifestation of assent to the offer's terms; the offeror is “master of the offer” and may define what qualifies. Acceptance must be on the same terms and unconditional, may be by promise or by performance, and silence ordinarily is not acceptance. It is effective on dispatch by reasonable means (except for options), and notification of acceptance by promise is ordinarily required.
edits.new: An acceptance is a manifestation of assent to the offer's terms; the offeror is “master of the offer” and may define what qualifies. Acceptance must be on the same terms and unconditional, may be by promise or by performance, and silence ordinarily is not acceptance. It is effective on dispatch by reasonable means (except for options), and notification of acceptance by promise is ordinarily required. Legal qualification: under Restatement § 63, an acceptance takes effect on dispatch only if it is made in a manner and by a medium the offer invites and the offer does not provide otherwise; an acceptance by an uninvited medium ordinarily takes effect only on receipt (C&M 262; § 67), one under an option only on receipt (§ 63(b)), and rejections and revocations take effect on receipt (§§ 40, 42). Silence accepts only in the cases § 69 lists; a reply that accepts while merely requesting a change still accepts unless it is made to depend on the change (§ 61); and notice of an acceptance by promise is not needed where the offer manifests a contrary intention (§ 56).
edits.reason: Slide 6 is recorded accurately, but its shorthand drops the conditions of the dispatch rule (§ 63 and C&M 262), the § 69 limits on silence, § 61, and § 56's exception.
